content: The exposure assessment for adults and children, including breastfed infants, is based on algorithms, default values, and unit exposures that establish the relationship between operational conditions and exposure. These parameters are derived from the Standard Operating Procedures for Residential Pesticide Exposure Assessments (USEPA, 2012) and the Exposure Factors Handbook: 2011 Edition (USEPA, 2011). Additional data sources include agricultural field-study databases and modeling approaches such as the European Predictive Operator Exposure Model (EUROPOEM, 2003) and the UK Predictive Operator Exposure Model (PSD, 2007). Users of these models are advised to modify default values on a case-by-case basis, replacing them with measured or improved estimates when available. Incorporating anthropometric and physiological datasets specific to the target population can enhance the accuracy of exposure predictions. The potential for an insecticide to cause adverse health effects depends on the route of exposure (ingestion, inhalation, dermal contact), the frequency and duration of exposure, the toxicity of the insecticide, and the sensitivity of the exposed individual. Exposure is also influenced by the amount of product or active ingredient handled and applied. Indoor residual spraying (IRS) exposure assessments involve multiple scenarios tailored to different target groups. For risk characterization, the total systemic dose must be calculated by summing all relevant exposure routes and pathways. The described exposure assessment serves as a first-tier approach, with higher-tier assessments using more complex methods, such as probabilistic risk assessment with uncertainty quantification, recommended when necessary. WHO has published guidance on exposure models and communicating uncertainties (WHO, 2005b; WHO, 2008). Special attention is given to unborn and newborn babies and children residing in sprayed houses due to their unique exposure patterns and potentially greater sensitivity to toxic chemicals. While this document provides a preliminary means of assessing risks to these sensitive groups, additional chemical-specific information is essential for improving risk assessment accuracy, particularly for unborn and newborn babies. Another area of uncertainty is the risk assessment of bioaccumulative active ingredients, such as DDT, where chemical-specific data on metabolism and toxicokinetics are critical. Assuming proper equipment calibration and adherence to safety instructions, exposure during IRS should generally be low. However, optimal conditions are not always maintained during spraying operations, and risk assessments assuming proper equipment and strict compliance may underestimate exposure levels. Unintentional misuse, such as contaminated clothing, perspiration on the skin, or the use of contaminated rags, is challenging to account for in models. These parameters are often impossible to quantify, and situations involving misuse or accidents are not covered in this document. Specific cases, such as pesticide container reuse or lactating mothers working as operators, should be considered separately, as they can be more reliably quantified than most misuse scenarios. Concurrent use of insecticides for agricultural purposes is also not accounted for in the model. Users of the models are strongly encouraged to incorporate case-dependent information when risky equipment or work patterns are known. Two scenarios are outlined: a guideline scenario, which assumes strict adherence to instructions, and a lax standard scenario, which allows for common deviations. Excessively high exposures from malfunctioning equipment or clear misuse are not covered in this risk assessment. General parameters for exposure assessment apply to both operator and residential exposure assessments. Chemical-specific or case-specific data should always be sought and used when possible. Risks for residents are estimated for adults, children (aged 6–11 years), toddlers (aged 12–24 months), and infants (aged <12 months), as recommended by the European Human Exposure Expert Group (HEEG, 2013a). Exposure via breast milk is estimated for infants and newborns (birth to 1 month). Anthropometric and physiological input parameters, such as weight, skin surface area, and ventilation rate, affect risk estimates. Ideally, data from the target population should be used, but the database must be internally consistent, covering all age groups and derived from the same population. The USEPA (2011) database is extensive and up-to-date, covering all age groups and relevant data points. It is recommended by HEEG (2013a) and was used in this document. For body weight, the 25th percentiles are applied; for respiration rate, HEEG recommendations are used. Adult spray operators and residents are assumed to weigh 60 kg. Toddlers aged 12–24 months are assumed to weigh 10 kg, and infants from birth to 12 months of age are assumed to weigh 8 kg. When appropriate anthropometric data are available for the population being assessed, these should be used. For example, weight and body surface area percentiles are based on females aged 30–40 years, 6–11 years, 12–24 months, and ≤12 months (USEPA, 2011; HEEG, 2013a). Mean values under moderate physical workload are used for ventilation rates. In the guideline scenario, WHO recommendations and product label instructions are assumed to be followed. WHO recommends that operators wear overalls for IRS. In the lax standard scenario, no personal protective equipment (PPE) other than light clothing covering the trunk is assumed. Tasks causing operator exposure include mixing and loading, application of the insecticide product by spraying, and washing and maintenance of the equipment. Products may be solids or liquids, with unit-dose packages expected to minimize operator exposure. Insecticides should be applied to achieve a uniform deposit on wall surfaces, requiring a constant spray flow from a nozzle held at a set distance from the wall. Spray should not be applied overhead, and high surfaces like ceilings may require an extended lance. Operator exposure duration is assumed to involve two rounds of insecticide spraying annually, working 8 hours a day, 6 days a week, with each round lasting 36 days. A single spray operator is assumed to apply 12 tank-loads of insecticide spray per day, with each tank-load containing 10 liters. The number of houses treated per day depends on the total area of sprayable surfaces, which may vary between 40 m² and 200 m². Proper maintenance procedures for spray equipment are assumed to prevent leakages during operations. Inhalation exposure during IRS is often low due to the low volatility of the insecticides used. However, aerosol with small droplet size may be generated, particularly when equipment without pressure regulation is used, increasing the risk of inhalation exposure. The risk is significant when compression sprayers are used at pressures of 3 bar or higher. In the guideline scenario, respiratory protection equipment (e.g., face masks) is assumed to provide 90% protection. In the lax standard scenario, no respiratory protective equipment is used. Dermal exposure in the lax standard scenario involves hands exposed to spray aerosol during application and to spray liquid during equipment washing and maintenance. In the guideline scenario, the sprayer is fully leak-proof, and protective clothing is assumed to provide 90% protection. Malfunctioning equipment, such as leaks or high spray pressure, may lead to very high exposure through both inhalation and dermal routes. Such misuse scenarios are not covered in this risk assessment. For residents, exposure is assumed to occur through skin contact with sprayed surfaces and contaminated food. Adults and older children are assumed to have similar exposure patterns, while toddlers have higher contact with the floor and hand-to-mouth activity. For infants, breast milk is an additional potential source of exposure. Misuse of empty product packages for storing food or drinking water may lead to high exposures and acute intoxications. These practices are highly variable and cannot be meaningfully modeled.
